fixes.explanation: Yes. The text says the sons of the prophets went to meet him and "…bowed down to the ground before him." That comes after they said, "The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha." They had been watching from Jericho when it all happened at the river.
Right. The fifty men "…searched for three days but did not find Elijah." Elisha had told them not to send anyone. When they came back, he said, "Didn't I tell you not to go?"

The text says the opposite. "…the waters there have been healthy to this day, according to the word spoken by Elisha." So the water didn't go bad again. The fix lasted, and the text ties it to Elisha's word.

Right. The text says, "…the waters there have been healthy to this day, according to the word spoken by Elisha." The water didn't go bad again. Elisha had said, "No longer will it cause death or unfruitfulness." Not a bad spring since.

Leading isn't on the table. The sons of the prophets at Bethel ask, "Do you know that the LORD will take your master away from you today?" That's about his master, not a job offer. I bet Elisha has enough on his plate without a promotion on top of it.

The prophets at Bethel do come out, but they come out to Elisha. They don't ask about Elijah speaking. They ask, "Do you know that the LORD will take your master away from you today?" No guest speaker on the schedule, friend, just a heads-up about today.

Not quite. When they ask, Elisha answers, "Yes, I know…" That's not how someone answers news that's brand new to them. Then he adds, "Do not speak of it." I think he's got a lot on his heart right then.

The cloak never goes flying. Elijah takes it, rolls it up, and strikes the waters with it. Then the waters part to the right and to the left. No throwing, just a rolled up cloak and a river that opens.
Nothing gets laid down on the bank. Elijah rolls up the cloak and strikes the waters with it. Then the waters part to the right and to the left, and the two of them cross over on dry ground.

Elisha says, "Please, let me inherit a double portion of your spirit…" Elijah had asked what he could do for him before being taken away, and that's the answer he got. I would've asked for a bigger oven. Elisha asked for something far better.

Not a long life. Elisha answers, "Please, let me inherit a double portion of your spirit…" He's asking for a share of Elijah's spirit, not extra years for himself. Elijah calls it "a difficult thing," so it's no small ask.

No blessing for the whole group here. Elisha's request is about Elijah's spirit: "Please, let me inherit a double portion of your spirit…" He says "let me," so he's asking for himself. Elijah answers that he has requested "a difficult thing."

Staying isn't the condition. Earlier Elijah does say, "Please stay here…" and Elisha keeps saying he will not leave him. But the condition for the double portion is about seeing: "…if you see me as I am taken from you, it will be yours."

The text doesn't use that word for the chariot. It says the chariot of fire with horses of fire "…separated the two of them…" Then Elijah went up into heaven in a whirlwind. The separating and the going up are two different lines in the verse.

The text doesn't say anything about leaving his clothes somewhere. It says, "…taking hold of his own clothes, he tore them in two." After that, the next thing we're told is that he picks up the cloak that had fallen from Elijah. Then he goes back and stands on the bank of the Jordan.

Elisha strikes the waters with Elijah's cloak and asks, "Where now is the LORD, the God of Elijah?" Elijah is out of sight, and the question isn't about Elijah. It's about the LORD. Then the waters part to the right and to the left, and Elisha crosses over.

Elisha doesn't ask about Elijah coming back. His question is, "Where now is the LORD, the God of Elijah?" Elijah's name is in there, but the LORD is who he asks about. When he struck the waters, they parted to the right and to the left.

That's not his question. The text gives his words: "Where now is the LORD, the God of Elijah?" It doesn't say why he asked it. I think it's a real question. And when he had struck the waters, they parted to the right and to the left.

Elijah coming back isn't in their words. The sons of the prophets say, "The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha." They said it after they saw what had happened at the river. Their words are about the man standing right in front of them.

Nobody says a word against the cloak. The sons of the prophets say, "The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha." Then they go to meet him and bow down to the ground before him. That's a welcome, friend, not a complaint.

The fifty men "…searched for three days but did not find Elijah." Three days is a long time to search and come back with nothing. I bet those were some tired feet. Elisha had said not to send them, and he reminded them when they got back.

Seven days is too long. The fifty men searched for three days, and they did not find Elijah. Then they went back to Elisha, who said, "Didn't I tell you not to go?" That's four days shorter than your guess, friend.
Forty days is far too long for this search. The fifty men searched for three days. They did not find Elijah. Forty days of searching would wear out a lot of sandals.
They never find him. The text says they "…searched for three days but did not find Elijah." So they came back with nothing. Then Elisha said, "Didn't I tell you not to go?"

Elisha says, "Bring me a new bowl, and put some salt in it." Then he goes out to the spring and casts the salt into it. It's a simple thing, salt in a bowl. And he says, "This is what the LORD says: 'I have healed this water…'"
Oil is a fair guess, but it isn't in this story. Elisha asks for a new bowl with salt in it. Then he goes out to the spring and casts the salt into it.
No sand in this story. Elisha asks for a new bowl with salt in it, and he casts the salt into the spring. Sand and salt might look alike in a bowl, but only one of them is in these verses.
